diveTitle: What actually happens when you convert to PDF
diveSubtitle: How fonts, tracked changes and comments are handled.
dive1Title: Fonts you don't have installed — how the PDF handles it
dive1Desc: Unlike opening a Word file, where a missing font gets silently substituted, converting to PDF embeds the actual font data into the file. That means the PDF looks correct on any device, even ones that don't have your fonts installed — one of the main reasons to convert in the first place.
dive2Desc: PDF conversion uses the final, accepted version of your document — tracked changes are automatically resolved and comment bubbles are dropped, since PDF has no equivalent editing-history layer. If you need reviewers' comments preserved, keep a separate .docx copy alongside the PDF.
dive3Desc: These convert exactly as they appear in Word, including different first-page headers or alternating odd/even headers if your document uses them. Page numbers convert as static text at their exact position — they won't auto-update if you later add pages to the PDF.
dive4Title: Embedded objects: tables, images, and charts
dive4Desc: An Excel table or chart pasted into Word converts as it currently displays — a snapshot of the data, not a live link. If the source spreadsheet changes later, the PDF won't reflect it; you'd need to update the Word doc and reconvert.
dive5Title: Documents with mixed page sizes or orientations
dive5Desc: If your Word document has sections with different page sizes or a mix of portrait and landscape pages, that's preserved page by page in the PDF output — each page keeps its own size and orientation exactly as set in Word's section breaks.
dive6Title: Why the PDF can look slightly different from the Word doc
dive6Desc: Minor rendering differences, like slightly different line spacing or how images anti-alias, can appear because Word and PDF use different rendering engines. The content and layout are the same — what you're seeing is a rendering-engine quirk, not data loss.
faqSubtitle: Got a question? We probably have the answer right here.
faq1Q: Is this Word to PDF converter free?
faq1A: Yes — you can use it for free, without creating an account and without watermarks. The free plan allows 5 uses per day and has a file-size limit; paid plans raise them.
faq2Q: Will my formatting survive the conversion?
faq2A: Yes. Our converter is built specifically to preserve Word formatting. Tables, bullet points, custom fonts, images, headers, footers, and page breaks all come through cleanly.
faq3Q: Is it safe to upload my documents here?
faq3A: Yes. All file transfers are encrypted (HTTPS). Your files are automatically deleted from our servers within 1 hour. We do not read your content.
faq4A: We support both .DOC (older Word format) and .DOCX (modern Word format). Files up to 5 MB are accepted on the free plan (20 MB on Starter).
faq5Q: Can I convert a Word file with images and tables?
faq5A: Yes. Images, tables, charts, and all embedded objects are fully supported. Everything that's in your Word document will appear in the PDF.
